chief_complaint: chronic bloating, loose stools, and extreme fatigue for 6 months
hpi_details: 6-month history of postprandial abdominal bloating, excessive flatulence, and 2-3 bulky, foul-smelling, pale stools per day. Reports profound fatigue and brain fog. Has an intensely itchy, blistering rash over both elbows for the past month. No blood in stool.
ideas: thinks she might be allergic to dairy or wheat after talking to friends
concerns: worried her constant fatigue is damaging her performance at her new job
expectations: wants blood tests for food intolerances and advice on supplements
pmh: type 1 diabetes since age 12, iron deficiency anaemia treated intermittently with oral iron
social_hx: non-smoker, drinks alcohol rarely, works as a graphic designer

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Coeliac Disease is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes Check coeliac serology while patient remains on a gluten-containing diet (critical instructions), adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chronic bloating, loose stools, and extreme fatigue for 6 months

Key HPI features: 6-month history of postprandial abdominal bloating, excessive flatulence, and 2-3 bulky, foul-smelling, pale stools per day. Reports profound fatigue and brain fog. Has an intensely itchy, blistering rash over both elbows for the past month. No blood in stool.

Objective/Exam findings: Check BMI, conjunctival pallor, inspect extensor rash on elbows. Serology: total IgE/IgA, anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTg IgA), FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, bone profile.
Relevant background/PMH: type 1 diabetes since age 12, iron deficiency anaemia treated intermittently with oral iron
Current medications: insulin glargine, insulin lispro
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Coeliac Disease.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Irritable bowel syndrome without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.

Ignoring critical warning signs such as: bloody or nocturnal diarrhoea, signs of severe malabsorption (marked weight loss, anaemia, low bone density), or persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet.
management_principles: Check coeliac serology while patient remains on a gluten-containing diet (critical instructions)
Refer for duodenal biopsy via gastroscopy for confirmation
Dermatology referral for skin biopsy if needed
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: 29F with T1DM presents with chronic steatorrhoea, bloating, fatigue, and an itchy extensor rash (dermatitis herpetiformis) over 6 months. History of iron deficiency anaemia.
reference_soap.objective: Check BMI, conjunctival pallor, inspect extensor rash on elbows. Serology: total IgE/IgA, anti-tissue transglutaminase (anti-tTg IgA), FBC, ferritin, folate, B12, bone profile.
reference_soap.assessment: Coeliac disease with likely dermatitis herpetiformis and malabsorption. DDx: irritable bowel syndrome, Giardia lamblia infection, inflammatory bowel disease, lactose intolerance.
reference_soap.plan: Check coeliac serology while patient remains on a gluten-containing diet (critical instructions). Refer for duodenal biopsy via gastroscopy for confirmation. Dermatology referral for skin biopsy if needed. Dietitian referral once confirmed.

learning_objectives: Identify autoimmune comorbidities associated with coeliac disease (Type 1 Diabetes, autoimmune thyroiditis)
Recognise extraintestinal manifestations of malabsorption (anaemia, dermatitis herpetiformis, fatigue)
Explain the critical importance of continuing gluten consumption prior to serological testing and biopsy
Address patient expectations regarding dietary modification and diagnostic accuracy

teaching.one_liner: An autoimmune reaction to gluten damages the small bowel lining, causing bloating, fatty pale stools, and malabsorption of nutrients like iron.
red_flags: Bloody or nocturnal diarrhoea — atypical for coeliac disease and should prompt evaluation for IBD
Signs of severe malabsorption (marked weight loss, anaemia, low bone density)
Persistent symptoms despite a gluten-free diet — raises concern for refractory coeliac disease

must_ask.say: Are your stools bulky, pale, and foul-smelling, and do they float?
Do your symptoms seem to get worse after eating bread, pasta, or other wheat foods?
Can you tell me about the rash on your elbows — is it itchy or blistering?
How would you describe the tiredness — is it affecting your concentration too?
Have you been told before that your iron levels are low?
Does anyone in your family have coeliac disease, diabetes, or thyroid problems?
